text: Every real organization has data scattered everywhere — a SQL Server database, a folder of CSV files, an app's API, a partner's FTP server. On its own, none of that raw data has the context to answer a real business question. Azure Data Factory is Microsoft's managed cloud service for exactly that job: moving and transforming all of it, at scale, without you having to build and babysit the servers that do the work.

Everything in Data Factory is built from five core pieces, and this entire course is really just these five ideas, explored in depth one chapter at a time. A linked service is a connection definition — like a connection string — telling Data Factory how to reach a specific data store or compute resource. A dataset points to the actual structure of data you want to use. An activity is a single processing step. A pipeline is a logical grouping of activities. And an integration runtime is the compute environment that actually executes all of it.

Here's what building one of these actually looks like once you're inside the tool itself. Factory Resources on the left lists every pipeline, dataset, and data flow you've built. The canvas in the middle is where you wire activities together — here, a Copy activity moving data from one dataset straight into another, with its source settings open right below it.

Microsoft frames how Data Factory works as four real stages, and nearly everything a data engineer actually does fits into one of them. Connect and collect reaches into on-premises and cloud sources alike, and moves raw data into one centralized store. Transform and enrich processes that collected data, either visually with mapping data flows or by calling out to compute services like Databricks. Publish loads the finished, business-ready result into a destination analytics tools can consume, following real CI/CD practice. And monitor tracks every single pipeline run's success and failure, with built-in support for alerts and logging.

Notice the natural build order here runs bottom-up, and it's worth memorizing exactly this way. You define a linked service to reach a data store. A dataset to describe the data sitting inside it. An activity to actually do something with that dataset. And a pipeline to group activities together into one single, manageable, monitorable unit.

Five components, four stages, one genuinely coherent platform built specifically for hybrid, at-scale data movement — not just another ETL script. Next: ETL versus ELT, and why swapping the order of those three letters changes where the real transformation work actually happens.
